sections.title: Nodes 0 & 1 — The problem before JavaScript, and values, types, and coercion
sections.content:
Where this sits

This is the base of the entire chain. Everything later — objects, closures, this, promises, the event loop — is built on the value model described here, and nearly every "JavaScript is weird" complaint you will ever hear traces back to a decision made in this node. Nothing depends on anything earlier, because there is nothing earlier.

Nodes 0 and 1 are elaborated together — Node 0 is purely the setup that makes Node 1 make sense.

Every term, from absolute zero

Server — a computer, owned by someone else, permanently connected to the internet, whose job is to hold files and hand them out when asked.

Client — the computer doing the asking. Your laptop. In web terminology the client is usually the browser specifically.

Browser — the program on your machine that asks servers for pages and draws them on screen. A browser is not a passive viewer; it is a large, complicated program that reads a document and decides how to paint it.

HTML — HyperText Markup Language. A text format for describing the structure of a document. HTML describes what things are, not what happens when you click them.

Round trip — one complete cycle of your computer sending a request to a server and receiving the reply. The important property is that it takes time you cannot avoid — the request has to physically travel to the server and the reply has to travel back.

Latency — the delay of that travel, measured in milliseconds. Distinct from bandwidth, which is how much data can flow per second.

Modem — the device that connected home computers to the internet over telephone lines in the 1990s, at speeds around 28,800 bits per second — roughly 3.5 kilobytes per second.

Form validation — checking that what someone typed into a form is acceptable before doing anything with it.

Interpreter — a program that reads source code and executes it directly, line by line. Contrast with a compiler, which translates all the source first into a different form that gets run later as a separate step. A language delivered over the network to run instantly cannot afford a build step, which pushed JavaScript toward interpretation.

Netscape — the company that made Netscape Navigator, the dominant web browser of the mid-1990s.

Brendan Eich — the programmer Netscape hired in 1995 to add a scripting language to their browser. He wrote the first version in about ten days in May 1995.

Java — a completely separate programming language, released by Sun Microsystems in 1995, extremely fashionable at that moment. It has essentially nothing to do with JavaScript. The name was borrowed for marketing.

Backward compatibility — the property that new versions continue to work with everything built for old versions. In JavaScript this is close to absolute, and it has a name in the standards community: "don't break the web."

Value — a single piece of data. The number 5. The text "hello". True.

Variable — a name that refers to a value. More precisely a binding: a connection between a name and a value.

Type — the kind of a value, which determines what operations make sense on it.

Dynamically typed — a language where a variable's type is not fixed in advance and is only known when the program runs. Contrast with statically typed, where types are declared or inferred and checked before the program runs.

Primitive — a value that is a single indivisible thing with no internal parts you can reach into and change. There are seven primitive types. The alternative is an object, a collection of named parts — Node 2's subject.

Bit — a single 0 or 1. The smallest possible piece of information.

Binary — counting using only 0 and 1, where each position is worth twice the one to its right.

Floating point — a way of storing numbers that can represent very large and very small values, and fractions, by storing significant digits alongside a separate exponent saying where the point sits. The point "floats" rather than being fixed.

IEEE 754 — the international standard, published in 1985, defining exactly how floating-point numbers are stored and how arithmetic on them behaves. Nearly every language implements it, which is why floating-point oddities are shared across languages rather than being JavaScript-specific.

Integer — a whole number with no fractional part. JavaScript has no separate integer type for ordinary arithmetic.

Unicode — the standard assigning a unique number, a code point, to every character in every writing system, plus emoji and symbols. About 1.1 million possible code points, roughly 150,000 currently assigned.

Code point — one Unicode number identifying one character, written like U+1F44B, where the digits are hexadecimal (base 16).

Code unit — the fixed-size chunk actually used to store text in a particular encoding. In UTF-16, which JavaScript strings use, each code unit is 16 bits. Small code points fit in one; large ones need two.

Immutable — cannot be changed after creation. Any operation that appears to change it produces a new value instead.

Coercion — automatic conversion of a value from one type to another, performed silently when an operation is given a type it didn't expect.

Truthy / falsy — how a value behaves where a true-or-false answer is required. A falsy value behaves as false; everything else is truthy. There are exactly eight falsy values.

typeof — a built-in operator returning text naming a value's type: "number", "string", "boolean", "undefined", "object", "function", "symbol", "bigint".

The history — why this exists at all

In 1994, a web page was a document and nothing more. The server sent HTML, the browser drew it, and the interaction ended. If a page contained a form, the only thing the browser could do with what you typed was package it up and send it back to the server. The server then examined it, and if the email address was missing an @, wrote an entirely new HTML page whose content was "invalid email address," and sent that back.

Over a 28,800-bit-per-second modem, that round trip took a noticeable, irritating second or more. And it happened per problem. If a form had four fields wrong, you discovered them one at a time, in four separate round trips, because the server would typically stop at the first failure. Filling in a form was an exercise in patience.

The obvious fix — let some code run inside the browser so that "does this contain an @" gets answered instantly — was obvious to everyone. But the constraints on such a language were unusual and they are what produced the language we have.

The code arrives as plain text, embedded in a page, from a server the user has never heard of. That means four things at once. It must begin executing essentially immediately, so there can be no compilation step the user waits through — which pushed hard toward an interpreter. It must be incapable of harming the machine it lands on, because it came from a stranger, so it gets no access to the filesystem and no ability to act outside the page. It must not be able to freeze the browser, because the browser has a page to draw. And — the constraint that outlasted all the others — it must never break existing pages, because there is no mechanism to go back and update the millions of pages already published by people who have moved on.

Netscape hired Brendan Eich in April 1995 and gave him roughly ten days in May to produce a working prototype. Ten days is not long enough to design a language. It is barely long enough to implement one you have already designed. The consequences are visible throughout: the language shipped with rough edges that were noticed almost immediately and could never be removed, because by the time anyone agreed they were mistakes, pages depended on them.

The name is pure marketing. The language was called Mocha internally, then LiveScript when it shipped in a Netscape beta in September 1995, and then renamed JavaScript in December 1995 as part of a partnership announcement with Sun Microsystems, whose Java language was the most fashionable thing in computing that year. The two languages are unrelated. This confusion is thirty years old and still generates interview questions.

One design decision from that period matters more than any other for this node. Eich was building a language for people writing small scripts in web pages — designers, hobbyists, people who were not professional programmers. A language that stopped and complained "you gave me text where I expected a number" would frustrate exactly that audience. So the language was built to keep going: when given a type it didn't expect, it would convert the value and carry on rather than failing. That is coercion, and it is the single most consequential decision in JavaScript's design. It made the language forgiving for beginners writing five-line scripts, and treacherous for professionals writing fifty-thousand-line applications — which is what everyone ended up doing.

The language was submitted to a standards body called Ecma International in 1996 and the first standard, ECMAScript, was published in June 1997. The name "JavaScript" was trademarked by Sun, so the standard needed a different one; that is why the specification and the language have different names. From 1997 onward, changing existing behaviour required convincing a committee that it wouldn't break the web — and it almost always would.

The mechanism — traced

How a number is actually stored

Every ordinary number in JavaScript occupies 64 bits, arranged according to IEEE 754's "double precision" format. Those 64 bits are divided into three fields:

  • 1 bit for the sign: 0 means positive, 1 means negative.
  • 11 bits for the exponent: roughly which power of two the number sits near.
  • 52 bits for the fraction (also called the mantissa or significand): the actual significant digits.

The value is reconstructed as roughly sign × 1.fraction × 2^(exponent − 1023). The 1023 is a fixed offset that lets the 11-bit exponent field represent both positive and negative exponents using only non-negative bit patterns.

Notice the leading 1. in that formula. Because any non-zero binary number can be written with exactly one 1 before the point, that leading digit is always 1 and therefore doesn't need storing. It is implied. So although only 52 bits are physically stored for the fraction, you get 53 bits of precision. That number, 53, governs everything else in this section.

Why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3

Write one-third in decimal and you get 0.3333… forever. It is not that decimal is broken; one-third simply has no exact finite decimal representation. Which fractions do terminate depends on the base you are writing in.

In base ten, a fraction terminates if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and 5. In base two, only 2. One-tenth is 1/10, and 10 = 2 × 5. That 5 is fatal: one-tenth has no exact binary representation. In binary it is 0.0001100110011001100…, repeating forever, exactly the way one-third repeats in decimal.

So when you write 0.1, the engine stores the closest value it can fit in 53 bits of precision. That value is not 0.1. It is:

0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

Similarly 0.2 is stored as a value slightly above two-tenths. Add those two slightly-wrong values and the errors compound rather than cancel, producing a result whose nearest 53-bit representation prints as 0.30000000000000004.

This is not a JavaScript bug. Java, C, C++, Python, C#, Ruby and Go all produce the same result, because they all use IEEE 754 doubles. What is JavaScript-specific is having no alternative — no integer type, no built-in decimal type — so you meet floating point even when doing arithmetic on whole numbers.

The practical consequence: never compare floating-point results with ===. Compare the absolute difference against a small tolerance instead. And never store money as a JavaScript number. Store it as a whole number of the smallest unit — paise, cents — which stays exact inside the safe integer range, and format for display at the last possible moment.

The safe integer limit

Whole numbers are stored in that same 53-bit precision. Any integer up to 2^53 fits exactly. Above that, there are more integers than 53 bits can distinguish, so the engine stores the nearest representable one — and above 2^53 the representable values are spaced two apart.

Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9,007,199,254,740,991, exactly 2^53 − 1. It is called safe because it is the largest integer n for which both n and n + 1 are exactly representable. Past it:

9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993  // true

Two different integers, indistinguishable, silently. Nothing throws.

This is not academic. Twitter's post IDs exceeded it in 2011 and every JavaScript client that parsed them as numbers silently corrupted them. Database primary keys of type bigint, timestamps in nanoseconds, and financial values in minor units all cross it routinely.

bigint, added in ES2020, is the fix: a separate primitive type for arbitrary-precision integers, written with an n suffix (9007199254740993n). It is exact at any size, but deliberately not interchangeable with number — mixing them in arithmetic throws a TypeError, precisely so you cannot accidentally launder an exact value through an inexact one.

Three special values also live in the number type. Infinity and -Infinity come from overflow or from dividing by zero — 1/0 is Infinity, not an error. And NaN, "not a number", is the result of arithmetic with no meaningful answer: 0/0, Math.sqrt(-1), Number("hello").

NaN has a property mandated by IEEE 754 that surprises everyone: it is not equal to itself. NaN === NaN is false. The reasoning is that NaN represents "the result of some failed computation," and two separate failures are not meaningfully "the same value." So you cannot test for NaN with ===. Use Number.isNaN(x). Do not use the older global isNaN(x) — it coerces its argument first, so isNaN("hello") is true even though "hello" is a string, not NaN.

There is also -0, negative zero, which exists because the sign bit is stored separately from the magnitude. -0 === 0 is true, but 1 / -0 is -Infinity while 1 / 0 is Infinity. Object.is(-0, 0) correctly reports false.

How a string is actually stored

A JavaScript string is a sequence of 16-bit code units, encoded in UTF-16.

When JavaScript was designed, Unicode was expected to need at most 16 bits per character — 65,536 possible characters seemed like plenty for every writing system. Several languages of that era, JavaScript and Java included, baked that assumption in. It turned out to be wrong. Unicode grew past 65,536, and UTF-16 was extended with a mechanism to encode larger code points using two 16-bit units, called a surrogate pair.

A range of code points, U+D800 through U+DFFF, was permanently reserved for this and assigned no characters of their own. A large code point is split across one "high surrogate" from U+D800–U+DBFF and one "low surrogate" from U+DC00–U+DFFF.

The waving-hand emoji is code point U+1F44B. That is far above 65,535, so it is stored as the pair 0xD83D 0xDC4B. And since .length counts code units, not characters:

"👋".length        // 2
"👋"[0]            // an unpaired surrogate — a broken half-character
[..."👋"].length   // 1 — spread uses the iteration protocol, which is code-point aware

This is why naive string truncation splits emoji in half and produces a replacement glyph. for...of, spread, and Array.from all iterate by code point and behave correctly; indexing and .length do not.

Strings are immutable. s[0] = "x" fails silently — it does nothing at all, and in strict mode it throws. Every string method returns a new string.

What coercion actually does

Coercion has two directions, and keeping them apart is most of the battle.

To boolean, when a value is used as a condition. Exactly eight values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else is truthy — including "0", the string "false", the empty array [], and the empty object {}. Arrays and objects are truthy because they are objects, and all objects are truthy regardless of contents. (There is exactly one bizarre exception, document.all in browsers, deliberately made falsy to keep 1990s pages working — a perfect illustration of "don't break the web.")

Between types, for comparison and arithmetic. == runs an algorithm the specification calls Abstract Equality Comparison:

  1. If both operands are the same type, compare them directly (identical to ===).
  2. If one is null and the other undefined, return true. This special case is why x == null is a legitimate idiom — it catches both, and nothing else.
  3. If one is a number and the other a string, convert the string to a number.
  4. If either is a boolean, convert it to a number first — true becomes 1, false becomes 0.
  5. If one is an object and the other a primitive, convert the object to a primitive by calling its valueOf(), and if that does not return a primitive, its toString().

Now trace the notorious [] == false, which is true even though [] is truthy:

  • false is a boolean, so by step 4 it becomes the number 0. Now: [] == 0.
  • [] is an object and 0 is a primitive, so by step 5 the array is converted. [].valueOf() returns the array itself, not a primitive, so [].toString() is used, producing the empty string "". Now: "" == 0.
  • String versus number, so by step 3 "" converts to the number 0. Now: 0 == 0, which is true.

There is no contradiction with [] being truthy. Truthiness asks "how does this behave as a condition"; == runs a conversion algorithm between two operands. Different questions, different rules — conflating them is what makes this feel arbitrary.

===, strict equality, skips all of it: different types means false, full stop. Use it always, with x == null as the one defensible exception.

Finally, typeof null returns "object". In the original 1995 implementation, values were stored as a small tag identifying the type plus the data itself; the tag for objects was zero, and null was represented as all zeros — so its tag read as "object". It was recognised as wrong almost immediately. A fix was formally proposed and rejected, because too much existing code checks typeof x === "object" in ways that would break. It is now permanent.

In your project

Stage 1 of shortlist walks you into most of this without asking. Job boards return payloads where some records have a location and some do not, so you will print undefined into a string and see it rendered as the literal text "undefined" — coercion to string, working exactly as designed and giving you nonsense. You will reach for job.salary || "Not listed" and it will be correct until a genuine 0 or "" shows up and gets overridden, which is the moment ?? stops being a syntax variant and becomes the tool that means what you meant.

Stage 5 is where the number model bites hardest. Once you are comparing and averaging salaries across currencies, doing it in floating point produces averages wrong in the last few digits and comparisons that fail at boundaries. The spec deliberately asks you to get this wrong once with floats and look at the output, then store everything as an integer number of minor units plus a currency code. Salary parsing also means reading "$120k" and "₹18,00,000" as numbers, which is parseInt versus Number territory: parseInt("120k") gives 120 by parsing leading digits and stopping, while Number("120k") gives NaN because it demands the entire string be numeric.

And the fingerprinting for deduplication is string work end to end — case folding, punctuation stripping, comparing "Senior Engineer" against "Sr. Engineer". If any company name in your dataset contains a character outside the basic range, .length-based truncation will split it.

In qbank

There is one honest connection worth knowing, and it is the kind of thing that impresses in an interview because almost nobody can explain it.

qbank uses Postgres through Drizzle. If any column in that schema is a Postgres bigint (a 64-bit integer, which can hold values far beyond 9,007,199,254,740,991), the underlying Node Postgres driver returns those values as strings, not numbers — and people routinely file this as a bug. It is not. The driver cannot return them as JavaScript numbers without risking silent corruption of any value above MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so it hands back a string and lets you decide. That decision exists purely because of the 53-bit precision limit traced above. Worth checking your actual schema to see whether you have any bigint columns, so you can speak about it concretely rather than in the abstract.

The other place this touches qbank is JSON coming back from the Anthropic API. Any number in a JSON payload becomes a JavaScript number when parsed, with the same precision limit — which is one reason IDs in APIs are so often strings rather than numbers.

What an interviewer does with this

"Why does 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3?" A weak answer is "floating point rounding errors" and stops. A strong answer explains that one-tenth has no exact binary representation because 10 has a prime factor of 5, that the stored value is therefore slightly off, that the errors compound when added, and — the part that separates candidates — that this is identical in Java, Python and C, so it is not a JavaScript quirk. Then add what you do about it: compare with a tolerance, store money as integer minor units.

"What's the difference between null and undefined?" A weak answer says "they're both empty." A strong one is precise about who assigns them: undefined is what the language supplies when nothing was provided; null is what a programmer assigns deliberately to mean "empty on purpose." Then mention that typeof null is "object", a 1995 implementation artefact kept for compatibility, and that x == null is the idiomatic check for both.

"What are the falsy values?" Recite all eight: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. The follow-up is usually "is [] falsy?" No — all objects are truthy. If they push on [] == false being true, walk the coercion steps.

"== or ===?" Always ===, because == runs a conversion algorithm whose results are hard to predict — except x == null, a well-understood idiom for catching both null and undefined. Being able to name the exception signals you know the rule rather than reciting advice.

"Why does JavaScript have bigint?" Because all ordinary numbers are 64-bit doubles with 53 bits of precision, integers stay exact only up to 2^53 − 1, and real-world values — database IDs, nanosecond timestamps, financial amounts in minor units — exceed that. Mentioning that bigint deliberately refuses to mix with number in arithmetic is the detail that shows you have actually used it.

sections.title: Node 2 — Objects, and the reference model
sections.content:
Where this sits

This node divides the language in half. Node 1 covered the seven primitive types; everything that is not one of those is an object, and objects follow completely different rules for copying, comparison, and assignment. Nodes 4 (closures), 6 (prototypes), 7 (collections), and 15 (memory leaks) all depend on understanding what a reference actually is, and the single most common category of real bug in working JavaScript code lives here.

Every term, from absolute zero

Object — a value that is a collection of named parts. Where a primitive is one indivisible thing, an object holds many things, each reachable by a name.

Property — one named part of an object. A property has a key (its name) and a value (what it holds).

Key — the name identifying a property. Keys can only be strings or symbols. Anything else used as a key is silently converted to a string first.

Object literal — the syntax for writing an object directly in source code, using curly braces: { a: 1, b: 2 }.

Dot notation — accessing a property by writing the key after a dot: user.name. Requires knowing the key when you write the code.

Bracket notation — accessing a property by writing an expression in square brackets: user["name"] or user[keyVariable]. Required whenever the key is computed or held in a variable.

Memory — the working storage a running program uses to hold values. You never manage it directly in JavaScript, but you need the word to talk about what a reference points at.

Reference — a value that identifies where something is stored rather than being the thing itself. If a primitive is a written number, a reference is a note saying "the number is in the third drawer." Copying the note gives you two notes pointing at one drawer, not two drawers.

Pass by value — the receiver gets an independent copy; changing it cannot affect the original. This is how all seven primitive types behave.

Pass by reference — the receiver gets a reference to the same underlying thing, so changes are visible everywhere. This is how all objects behave.

Mutation — changing an object in place while it remains the same object. Distinct from reassignment, which points a variable at an entirely different value.

Identity — whether two references point to the same underlying object. Distinct from structural equality, which asks whether two objects have the same contents. JavaScript's === tests identity for objects, never structure.

Shallow copy — a new object whose top-level properties are copied. Any property whose value was itself an object is copied as a reference, so both objects still share that nested object.

Deep copy — a new object where every level of nesting has been duplicated independently, sharing nothing with the original.

Circular reference — an object that, following its properties, eventually leads back to itself. a.self = a is the simplest case. Circular references break naive copying and break JSON.stringify.

Nullish — meaning null or undefined, and specifically not the other falsy values. The word exists because operators added in 2020 needed a name for exactly that pair.

Short-circuit — an operator that stops evaluating as soon as the answer is determined. In a || b, if a is truthy the answer is a and b is never evaluated.

Enumerable — a property that shows up when you list an object's keys. Properties you write normally are enumerable; some built-in ones deliberately are not. This is the shallow version of Node 16's material.

The history — why this exists at all

Node 1 gave you individual values. That is enough to write a calculator and nothing else. The moment you want to represent a person, an order, a job posting, or an HTTP request, you need to hold several values together and be able to say which is which.

The two classic answers in programming languages are the record — a fixed set of named fields, declared in advance, checked by the compiler — and the dictionary (or hash map, or associative array) — an open-ended collection of key-value pairs you can add to and remove from at runtime. Records are what C structs and Java classes give you: rigid, fast, checked. Dictionaries are what Python's dict and Perl's hashes give you: flexible, dynamic, unchecked.

JavaScript, being dynamically typed and designed in ten days for people writing small scripts, went entirely with the dictionary. There is no declaration step, no fixed field list, no check. An object is a bag of key-value pairs, and you may add a property at any moment, delete one, or ask for one that was never there — the last of which returns undefined rather than failing. That decision is why user.emial is a legal expression that quietly evaluates to undefined instead of an error, which is the exact failure mode Node 18 eventually names as the language's core limitation.

The consequential decision, though, is not the dictionary shape — it is how objects are handled when you move them around. Here JavaScript followed a convention nearly every language of its lineage shares: primitives are copied, objects are shared. The reason is practical. An object can be arbitrarily large. If passing one to a function meant duplicating the whole thing, every call carrying an object would be expensive, and there would be no way for a function to modify a structure its caller can see. So what actually gets passed is a small reference, and everyone holding a reference is looking at the same object.

This is genuinely the right engineering trade, and it is also the source of an enormous fraction of real bugs, because the sharing is invisible. Nothing in the syntax distinguishes const b = a where a is a number from const b = a where a is an object, but the first gives you independence and the second gives you an alias.

One more piece of history matters. The 2015 standard added spread syntax ({...obj}) and 2017 finished the object utilities, and together these made a particular style popular: instead of mutating an object, build a new one with the changes applied. This "treat objects as immutable" discipline arrived largely from the React ecosystem, where change detection depends on comparing object identity cheaply — if you mutate an object in place, its identity is unchanged and nothing can tell anything happened. That is why setState({...state, count: 5}) looks the way it does.

The mechanism — traced

What an object actually is

const user = { name: "Devansh", city: "Noida" };

Three things happened. An object was created in memory, holding two properties. A reference to that object was produced. And the name user was bound to that reference. The variable user does not contain the object — it contains a reference to it. This distinction is invisible in the syntax and it is the whole node.

Keys are strings or symbols, and only those:

const obj = {};
obj[1] = "a";
obj["1"] = "b";
obj[1];              // "b" — the same property
Object.keys(obj);    // ["1"] — one key, a string

The number 1 was converted to the string "1", so both writes hit one property. This is why Map exists (Node 7) — it accepts keys of any type without converting them.

Arrays follow directly. An array is an object whose keys are the string forms of consecutive integers, plus a length the engine maintains:

const arr = ["a", "b"];
typeof arr;          // "object"
Object.keys(arr);    // ["0", "1"]
arr["0"];            // "a"

typeof cannot distinguish an array from a plain object, which is why Array.isArray() exists. Functions are objects too, with the one carve-out that typeof reports "function" — a special case in the specification, not derivable from the rules. Dates, regular expressions, Map, Set, and Error instances are all objects as well.

Dot versus bracket

user.name          // key written literally in the source
user["name"]       // identical result
const k = "name";
user[k]            // the only way to use a key held in a variable
user.k             // WRONG — looks for a property literally named "k"

Bracket notation is also required for keys that are not valid identifiers — obj["first name"], obj["2fa-enabled"].

The reference model, demonstrated

let a = 5;
let b = a;
b = 10;
a;   // 5 — completely unaffected

b received a copy of the value. There is no connection.

const a = { count: 5 };
const b = a;
b.count = 10;
a.count;   // 10 — the SAME object was modified

b received a copy of the reference. Both names point at one object. There is only ever one object here.

function addTag(job) {
  job.tags = ["remote"];      // mutates the caller's object
}
function replace(job) {
  job = { tags: ["remote"] }; // rebinds the local parameter only
}

addTag changes what the caller sees. replace does not — it pointed the local name at a brand new object, leaving the caller's reference untouched. This is why the precise description is "pass by value, where the value being passed is a reference." Reassigning the parameter does nothing outward; mutating through it does.

Why const is weaker than it looks

const user = { name: "Devansh" };
user.name = "changed";     // fine
user.role = "engineer";    // fine
user = {};                 // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

const freezes the binding — the connection between the name and the reference. It says nothing about the object. const arr = []; arr.push(1) is legal for exactly this reason.

const user = Object.freeze({ name: "Devansh", address: { city: "Noida" } });
user.name = "x";              // silently ignored (throws in strict mode)
user.address.city = "Delhi";  // WORKS — freeze is shallow

Object.freeze prevents adding, removing, or changing the object's own properties. It does not touch nested objects, because those are separate objects reached through a reference.

Equality is identity

const a = { x: 1 };
const b = { x: 1 };
const c = a;

a === b;   // false — two different objects
a === c;   // true  — same object

=== on objects asks one question: are these the same object? It never inspects contents. There is no built-in deep equality — your options are a recursive comparison, a library, or (only for simple JSON-safe data) comparing JSON.stringify output, which is fragile because key order matters.

This identity rule is also why the immutable-update style exists. If you mutate an object in place its identity is unchanged, so code that cached the old reference and compares with === concludes nothing happened. Build a new object instead, and the identity change is the signal.

Copying, and the shallow/deep boundary

const original = { name: "Devansh", address: { city: "Noida" } };

const shallow = { ...original };
shallow.name = "changed";
original.name;          // "Devansh" — top level is independent

shallow.address.city = "Delhi";
original.address.city;  // "Delhi" — nested object is SHARED

The spread copied two properties: the string (a primitive — copied by value) and the reference to the address object (copied as a reference). One new outer object was created; the inner object was never duplicated. Object.assign({}, original) does exactly the same thing.

const deep = structuredClone(original);
deep.address.city = "Delhi";
original.address.city;  // "Noida" — untouched

structuredClone is built in, available in Node 17+ and all current browsers. It handles arbitrary nesting, Map, Set, Date, RegExp, typed arrays, and circular references, which naive recursive copying loops forever on. What it cannot clone: functions, DOM nodes, and class instances lose their prototype and come back as plain objects. A function throws DataCloneError — the same error you meet in Stage 6 of shortlist, because workers use the same cloning algorithm.

The old trick JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) also deep-copies, badly: it destroys Date objects into strings, drops undefined and functions, throws on circular references, and cannot represent Map or Set.

The utilities you will actually use

Object.keys(user)     // ["name", "city"] — own enumerable string keys
Object.values(user)   // ["Devansh", "Noida"]
Object.entries(user)  // [["name","Devansh"], ["city","Noida"]]

Object.entries is what lets you iterate an object with array methods, and it pairs with Object.fromEntries to go back — the standard value transform is Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).map(([k, v]) => [k, f(v)])).

"name" in user                  // true — includes inherited properties (Node 6)
Object.hasOwn(user, "name")     // true — own properties only
user.name !== undefined         // WRONG — a property explicitly set to undefined exists

Object.hasOwn (ES2022) replaces the older user.hasOwnProperty("name"), which breaks if an object has a property literally named hasOwnProperty.

Optional chaining and nullish coalescing

Before 2020, safely reading a nested value meant a chain of guards: user && user.address && user.address.city. Optional chaining collapses it:

const city = user?.address?.city;   // undefined if any link is null/undefined

?. checks whether the value to its left is null or undefined; if so the whole expression short-circuits to undefined instead of throwing. It works for calls (obj.method?.()) and bracket access (arr?.[0]). It guards only against nullish values, and should not be sprayed everywhere — using it on something that should never be missing hides bugs rather than handling them.

const count = job.applicants || 10;   // gives 10 when applicants is 0 — WRONG
const count = job.applicants ?? 10;   // gives 0 when applicants is 0 — correct

?? supplies the right-hand value only when the left is null or undefined. This is the single most common real bug it was introduced to fix: legitimate 0, "", and false values being silently replaced by defaults. There is also ??=, which assigns only if the target is nullish.

In your project

This node is load-bearing across three stages of shortlist.

In Stage 1, the || versus ?? distinction arrives immediately. Job payloads have fields that are legitimately 0 (applicant count) or "" (an empty location meaning "unspecified"), and job.salary || "Not listed" will override them wrongly.

In Stage 2, the spec warns that when you dedupe later you will find you have been mutating the same raw object from two adapters. That is this node arriving as a bug. The fix is either never mutating raw at all or structuredClone-ing it at the adapter boundary, and choosing between those is a real decision with a real cost.

In Stage 5, deduplication is entirely about identity versus structure. Two records from two boards are structurally similar and never ===, so you build a fingerprint string and use it as a Map key — replacing identity comparison with a structural one you defined yourself. Merging duplicates is the {...a, ...b} pattern, later keys winning.

In Stage 6, structuredClone's limits become a hard error: sending data to a worker uses the same algorithm, so passing a class instance with methods gets you a DataCloneError or a stripped plain object. That is the moment to realise a Source adapter cannot cross the worker boundary — only its plain data can.

In qbank

Anything qbank does with Drizzle returns plain objects from the database, and any code that takes one of those rows and mutates it — adding a computed field, normalising a value — is mutating a shared object if that reference was handed anywhere else. Worth grepping for places that modify a query result in place, because that is precisely where a hard-to-see bug lives.

The more interesting one: qbank's Anthropic integration uses forced tool use, receiving structured JSON arguments back from the model. Those arrive as freshly parsed plain objects, and anything done to them before validation — merging defaults, filling missing fields — is object manipulation of exactly this kind. When you read that code to explain it, the question to ask is "does this mutate the model's response or build a new object from it," because the answer determines whether the raw response is still intact by the time you log it.

What an interviewer does with this

"Is JavaScript pass by value or pass by reference?" A trap with a precise answer. JavaScript is always pass by value — but for objects, the value being passed is a reference. So mutating through the parameter affects the caller, while reassigning the parameter does not. Stating both halves, with the two-function example, is a strong signal.

"Does const make an object immutable?" No. It prevents reassigning the binding. Immutability needs Object.freeze, and even that is shallow.

"Why is {a:1} === {a:1} false?" Because === on objects compares identity, not structure. Follow up by noting there is no built-in deep equality, and that JSON.stringify comparison is a crude substitute that breaks on key ordering, dates, and anything JSON cannot represent.

"How do you deep clone an object?" structuredClone — it handles nesting, Map, Set, Date, and circular references. Then name its limits: functions and class prototypes do not survive. Mentioning that JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is the old approach and listing what it destroys shows you know the trade.

"What's the difference between || and ???" || falls back on any falsy value; ?? only on null and undefined. The concrete example lands: a legitimate 0 or "" silently replaced by a default, which is the bug ?? was added in ES2020 to fix.
